lessons.title: Count outcomes and events
lessons.summary: Count ordered outcomes only when they are equally likely.
lessons.body:
Probability describes uncertainty in a specified experiment. Before counting, decide what one outcome records. A request might succeed or fail; two dice produce a pair of face values, not just a total.

## Choose outcomes before counting

The **sample space** contains all possible outcomes. A **random event** is a set of outcomes we care about: for example, all dice pairs whose total is seven. A probability assigns an event a number between zero and one.

Counting gives a probability only in a finite nonempty space whose outcomes are equally likely. Otherwise each outcome needs its own weight. Two labels such as “success” and “failure” do not imply equal chances.

With two independent fair six-sided dice, there are 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Seven is a more likely total than two because six pairs make seven and only one makes two. The totals themselves are not equally likely.

```formula reference
P(A) = |A| / |Ω|
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
P(A): the probability of event A, a number from 0 to 1; probability zero need not mean an impossible outcome in an infinite model
A: the event we care about, written as the set of outcomes that count as "A happened"
Ω: omega, the sample space: the set of every possible outcome
|A|: the number of outcomes in A (vertical bars around a set mean "how many elements it has")
|Ω|: the total number of possible outcomes
In words: When every outcome is equally likely, an event’s probability is its share of all outcomes.
```

The formula is a counting shortcut after the model is justified. A loaded die needs different weights even though its face labels are unchanged.

## Do not merge unequal categories

First-die one and second-die six differs from first-die six and second-die one. Combining them into an unordered pair creates a category with two ways to occur; a double such as three and three has only one. Treating those categories as equally likely changes the model.

## Key takeaways
- Define the experiment and its outcomes before counting.
- Equal labels do not imply equal probabilities.
- Preserve order when the experiment distinguishes positions.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Combine events without double-counting
lessons.summary: Subtract the overlap when combining events.
lessons.body:
Combining failure rates starts with a practical question: can the same request appear in both groups? If so, simply adding the rates counts some requests twice.

## Combine events carefully

Probability is never negative, the whole sample space has probability one, and probabilities add for events that cannot happen together. Such events are **disjoint**. The addition axiom also covers countably many pairwise disjoint events; infinite models restrict probabilities to a specified collection of measurable events.

For overlapping events, the **addition rule** adds their probabilities and subtracts the probability of their overlap once. “Either” includes cases where both happen. For example, a request that is both slow and erroneous belongs in the union once, not twice.

The **complement** is everything outside an event. Its probability is what remains from one. This often makes “at least one failure” easier: work out the chance of no failures first.

## A bound when overlap is unknown

The **union bound** adds the individual probabilities without subtracting overlap. It cannot underestimate the probability that at least one event happens, and it requires no independence assumption. It may overestimate badly when failures occur together.

```formula reference
P(B_1 ∪ B_2 ∪ … ∪ B_n) ≤ n × p
where
B_1, B_2, …, B_n: n "bad" events, for example "request i hits a slow server"
n: how many bad events there are
p: an upper limit on each bad event's probability, so P(B_i) ≤ p for every i
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
∪: union, "at least one of these happens"
…: and so on, for every event in between
≤: less than or equal to
In words: the chance that any bad event occurs is at most the event count times a shared upper bound on each event's probability, whether or not the events are independent.
```

If the sum exceeds one, use one as the trivial upper bound: probabilities cannot exceed certainty. The bound is useful for budgeting many small risks, not for claiming their exact combined probability.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: overlapping guest lists
> Two organisers count their invitees, but some people appear on both lists.
>
> **How it maps:** Adding list sizes counts shared guests twice; subtracting the overlap counts each invited person once.
>
> **Where it stops:** Unequally likely outcomes need probability weights, not just headcounts.

## Key takeaways
- Subtract overlap to obtain an exact union probability.
- Adding probabilities gives an upper bound without independence.
- A bound above one provides no useful extra information.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Condition on evidence and draw sequences
lessons.summary: Condition only on events with positive probability.
lessons.body:
Evidence changes which outcomes are still possible and how they are weighted. **Conditional probability** asks about an event within the cases where the evidence holds.

## Change the group you are considering

Suppose two independent fair dice total eight. The remaining ordered pairs are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2). A first die of one is now impossible, and a first die of three occurs in one of the five remaining cases. Using the original six-face probability would ignore the evidence.

```formula reference
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
P(A | B): the probability of A given B; the vertical bar | is read "given" and means "once we know B happened"
A: the event we are asking about
B: the event we already know happened; P(B) must be greater than 0
P(A ∩ B): the probability that A and B both happen (∩ means "and", both together)
P(B): the probability of B
In words: Restrict attention to the positive-probability evidence and ask what fraction of those cases also satisfy the event of interest.
```

This elementary ratio requires a conditioning event with positive probability. In infinite models, a possible event can have probability zero; conditioning there requires a more general construction.

## Sequences change their own conditions

For two events to happen together, the **multiplication rule** combines the chance of the first with the chance of the second given the first. It does not assume independence.

Draw cards from a uniformly shuffled standard deck without replacement. After drawing an ace, there are fewer aces and fewer cards left. The second draw must use that changed deck. Reusing the original ace probability would model replacement instead.

The same reasoning applies to retries: if the first failure indicates an outage, the next attempt may have a different success chance. Multiplying unchanged per-attempt chances is justified only when the model supports it.

## Key takeaways
- Conditioning changes the reference group to cases consistent with evidence.
- Sequence probabilities use the updated condition at each step.
- Without replacement, an earlier draw changes the next draw's chances.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Weight cases with total probability
lessons.summary: A partition covers every outcome exactly once.
lessons.body:
An overall error rate depends on both regional error rates and how much traffic each region serves. Giving a tiny region the same weight as a busy one answers the wrong question.

## Weight cases by how often they occur

A **partition of the sample space** separates outcomes into disjoint cases that cover everything exactly once. The **law of total probability** finds an overall chance by weighting its chance within each case by the chance of that case. Zero-probability cases can be omitted; a finite or countable partition supports this sum.

If most requests go to a reliable region, the overall rate lies nearer that region's rate. Moving more traffic to an unreliable region raises the overall error rate even if neither regional rate changes.

```formula reference
P(A) = Σ_i P(A | B_i) × P(B_i)
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
P(A): the overall probability of event A
B_i: the i-th piece of the partition, for example "the request went to region i"
i: an index counting the pieces 1, 2, 3, …
Σ_i: sigma, "add up the following term for every piece i"
P(A | B_i): the probability of A given that we are in piece B_i (| is read "given")
P(B_i): the probability of landing in piece B_i
In words: the overall event probability is a weighted average of its probability within each disjoint case, weighted by how often each case occurs.
```

The cases must refer to the same experiment and cover it without overlap. Averaging regional percentages equally would instead describe a uniformly selected region.

## The observation policy matters

In the three-door game, a car is initially equally likely behind each door. After your choice, a knowledgeable host always reveals an unchosen goat and offers a switch. Switching wins whenever your original choice was wrong: two out of three games.

If the host also chooses fairly when two goat doors are available, switching still has a two-thirds chance after observing a particular door opened. To condition on that observation, weight each car location by how likely that location makes the host's action.

A host who opens an unchosen door blindly and happens to reveal a goat follows a different policy. Under uniform blind choice, the two unopened doors are equally likely conditional on that observation. The visible goat alone does not specify the experiment.

## Key takeaways
- Weight conditional rates by the size of each disjoint case.
- A changed mixture can change an overall rate without changing any component rate.
- Include the observation policy in the probability model.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Test independence and use complements
lessons.summary: Independence is an equality of probabilities.
lessons.body:
Two events are **independent** when learning that one occurred leaves the chance of the other unchanged, whenever that conditioning event has positive probability. Physical separation does not establish this property.

## Independence is a model claim

```formula essential
P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)
P(A | B) = P(A)   if P(B) > 0
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
A, B: two events
P(A ∩ B): the probability that both A and B happen
P(A), P(B): the separate probabilities of A and of B
P(A | B): the probability of A given that B happened (| is read "given")
In words: two events are independent when the chance of both is the product of their chances; equivalently, learning that B happened leaves A's chance unchanged.
```

This relationship distinguishes independence from mere lack of an obvious connection. Two events can share parts of an experiment and still be independent.

For independent fair dice, knowing the total is seven leaves the first die equally likely to show any face. Knowing the total is eight rules out a first die of one, changing its distribution. Check the relevant probabilities rather than the names of the events.

**Disjoint** events with positive probabilities are dependent: learning that one happened rules out the other. “Cannot happen together” is different from “learning one changes nothing”.

## At least one means not none

For several calls, “at least one slow” is the complement of “all fast”. If the calls are mutually independent, multiply their fast probabilities and subtract the result from one. Directly adding slow probabilities generally double-counts cases with several slow calls.

Adding more independent calls with a nonzero chance of slowness increases the chance of encountering at least one slow call. It does not make a slow call certain for any fixed finite number when each can still be fast.

If calls share an overloaded backend, the complement identity still holds. It is the multiplication of unchanged probabilities that needs reconsideration. Pairwise independence alone is insufficient for multiplying an entire sequence.

## Key takeaways
- Independence concerns probabilities, not physical separation.
- Positive-probability disjoint events are dependent.
- Complement reasoning is general; multiplying across calls needs the appropriate independence.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Model series and redundant availability
lessons.summary: Series systems require every component to work.
lessons.body:
Availability asks whether a service is working at a sampled instant, or what fraction of time it is serving. The first modelling decision is which components must be working together.

## Required dependencies versus alternatives

In a **series system**, every required component must work. A checkout path needing a gateway, authentication and payment service fails when any required link fails. Adding another required dependency cannot improve availability in this model. With independent component states, multiply their availabilities. When at least two required components each have availability strictly between zero and one, the path is less available than either one alone.

In **parallel redundancy**, any one replica is sufficient. With perfect routing and failover and no other failure causes, the service fails only when all replicas are down. Under mutual independence, multiply the downtime probabilities and take the complement. This can produce a large improvement, but the assumptions do the work.

## Investigate shared failure causes

Replicas can share power, networking, configuration or a software defect. A bad change rolled out everywhere may take every copy down together. A surviving replica may also overload when traffic shifts to it. Both mechanisms break the independent-failure model.

Separating failure domains reduces some shared infrastructure risks; it does not remove shared software risks. Review routing, failover capacity and deployment practice before using a replica count to promise an availability target.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: keys and spare keys
> A journey needing every key on a ring stops if one required key is missing. Spare copies of one key help only if one copy can still be reached.
>
> **How it maps:** Required keys resemble series dependencies; usable copies resemble redundant replicas. Losing the bag containing every copy is a shared failure.
>
> **Where it stops:** Services also have partial failures, recovery delays and changing capacity; physical keys do not model those dynamics.

## Key takeaways
- Decide whether all components or any one component must work.
- Multiplication assumes independent component states.
- Shared causes and inadequate failover can defeat redundancy.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Check a model by simulation and enumeration
lessons.summary: Enumeration is exact for finite equally likely outcomes.
lessons.body:
A simulation samples outcomes from a model; enumeration lists every outcome. Both can catch reasoning errors, but neither establishes that the model represents the real system.

## Sample a model

The code models independent fair die rolls and records whether any of four rolls is a six. Each experiment produces one yes/no observation.

```python
import random

def at_least_one_six(rolls=4):
    # Stop as soon as one roll is a six.
    return any(random.randint(1, 6) == 6
               for _ in range(rolls))

trials = 1_000_000
# Count successful simulated experiments.
hits = sum(at_least_one_six()
           for _ in range(trials))
print(hits / trials)   # about 0.518
```

The printed fraction varies between runs. With independent identically distributed experiments it approaches the model probability as the sample grows, but it need not move closer after every extra trial.

## Enumerate when the space is small

```python
from itertools import product
from fractions import Fraction

dice = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
# Restrict the space to the known sum.
sum8 = [d for d in dice if sum(d) == 8]
# Count favourable outcomes within it.
first3 = [d for d in sum8 if d[0] == 3]
print(Fraction(len(first3), len(sum8)))
# 1/5
```

Here every ordered dice pair is equally likely. Filtering to the known total changes the denominator as well as the numerator. The fraction is exact for this model because every permitted outcome is included, rather than sampled.

## Choose an appropriate check

Enumeration becomes expensive as the outcome space grows. Simulation scales more readily, but rare events may be missed entirely in a finite run. Seeing no failures is not proof that their probability is zero.

The **standard error** describes variation between estimates. For independent yes/no trials, increasing the trial count fourfold halves the standard error; it does not guarantee a particular realised error. Small relative errors for rare probabilities can require many trials.

If real retries share an outage while the simulation gives each an independent fresh chance, more simulation only estimates the wrong model more precisely. Test the assumptions against observations too.

## Key takeaways
- Enumeration is exact when the outcomes and weights are fully specified.
- Simulation estimates a model probability with sampling variation.
- Rare events and incorrect assumptions need special care.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Update beliefs with Bayes’ theorem
lessons.summary: The posterior combines likelihood and prior, then normalises by the evidence.
lessons.body:
A detector catching most fraud does not mean most of its alerts are fraud. One statement starts with fraudulent payments; the other starts with flagged payments. **Bayes’ theorem** connects those different reference groups.

## Reweight competing explanations

Start with a **prior probability**: how plausible each explanation is before this evidence. For each explanation, ask how likely it would make the evidence: its **likelihood**. Combine prior and likelihood, then normalise across the possible explanations. The result is a **posterior**.

```formula essential
P(H | E) = (P(E | H)P(H)) / P(E)
where
H: a positive-probability hypothesis, for example "this patient is ill" or "this payment is fraud"
E: the observed event, for example "the test came back positive"; its probability must be positive
P(H): the **prior probability** (the prior), your belief in H before seeing the evidence (often the base rate)
P(E | H): the **likelihood term** (the likelihood), how expected the evidence is if H is true (| is read "given")
P(E): the **evidence term**, how common the evidence is overall, from every cause
P(H | E): the **posterior**, your belief in H after seeing the evidence
P: probability, from 0 to 1; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: Reweight the prior by how likely the hypothesis makes the evidence, then normalise by the evidence probability across all explanations.
```

The denominator counts every way the evidence can arise, including false alerts. The elementary update needs positive evidence probability; the displayed likelihood also needs a positive prior for its conditioning hypothesis.

## A strong detector can still have many false alerts

Imagine fraudulent payments are rare. Even a small false-positive rate applied to the much larger legitimate population can generate more alerts than correctly detected fraud. A flag can raise the probability of fraud substantially while leaving fraud less likely than a false alarm.

Ignoring the prior is the **base-rate fallacy**. Ignoring how often legitimate cases trigger the evidence is another way to lose the comparison. Neither the detection rate alone nor the prior alone determines the posterior.

Within a fixed model, positive-probability evidence cannot revive a hypothesis assigned prior probability zero. Evidence the model declares impossible makes this elementary update undefined; revisit the model rather than dividing by zero.

## Key takeaways
- Prior, likelihood and posterior describe different stages of reasoning.
- Include all explanations for the observed evidence.
- A detection rate is not the probability that an alert is genuine.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Interpret a positive test using counts
lessons.summary: Sensitivity is not the chance of illness after a positive result.
lessons.body:
Use counts to see which group a test result refers to. This is a hypothetical probability model, not an assessment of an individual medical result.

## Start from the whole population

Suppose a condition affects 1% of a population. A test detects 99% of affected people: its **sensitivity**. It also flags 5% of unaffected people: its **false positive rate**. Its **specificity**, the proportion of unaffected people testing negative, is 95%.

The expected counts in a hypothetical group of 10,000 are:

| Group | Expected positive | Expected negative |
|---|---|---|
| 100 affected | 99 | 1 |
| 9,900 unaffected | 495 | 9,405 |

These are model expectations; an actual group need not contain precisely these counts.

## Now restrict attention to positive results

Among the 594 expected positives, only 99 are affected: about one in six. The many unaffected people produce more false positives even though each has a relatively small chance of testing positive.

Sensitivity asks about results among affected people. **Positive predictive value**, also called precision, asks about affected people among positive results. Specificity asks about negative results among unaffected people. Changing the denominator changes the question.

The positive result still provides evidence: the model probability rises above the original 1%. “Most positives are false” does not mean the test tells us nothing. Its interpretation depends on prevalence and both conditional test rates.

## Key takeaways
- Keep the reference group explicit when interpreting a percentage.
- Compare expected true and false positives within the positive group.
- Expected counts explain the model, not guaranteed individual outcomes.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Interpret rare-event alerts
lessons.summary: Precision depends on prevalence as well as conditional detection rates.
lessons.body:
An alert queue can be mostly false alarms even when a detector catches nearly every real problem. Whether this happens depends on the base rate and false-positive rate together.

## Measure the decision you actually face

**Classifier recall** (usually shortened to recall) or sensitivity is the share of real cases detected. **Classifier precision** (usually shortened to precision) is the share of alerts that are real. **Classification accuracy** is the share of all predictions that are correct. On strongly imbalanced data, always predicting the common class can achieve high accuracy while finding none of the rare cases.

A fraud team deciding which alerts to investigate needs precision as well as sensitivity. A rare cause creates many more opportunities for false alerts than true ones, so a small false-positive rate may dominate the queue. Rarity alone does not imply poor precision: a detector with no false positives is a counterexample.

## Compare changes under explicit assumptions

When true and false alerts both occur, holding sensitivity and prevalence fixed while reducing false positives improves precision. Holding positive sensitivity and a positive false-positive rate fixed, increasing prevalence within a mixed population also improves precision. With no false positives, precision is already perfect whenever alerts occur. If sensitivity is already near perfect and false alerts dominate, a tiny sensitivity improvement has little effect on queue quality.

Real threshold changes often trade sensitivity against false positives. A filter selecting a higher-risk population can change both conditional rates. Re-estimate them in that population instead of assuming only the prevalence changed.

Daily true and false alert counts predicted by a model are expectations, not a promise for every day's queue. Combine rate measurements with investigation costs and the consequences of missed cases.

## Key takeaways
- Detection rate, precision and accuracy answer different questions.
- Base rates matter even when detector rates are known precisely.
- Re-estimate rates after a threshold or population change.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Update odds and repeated evidence
lessons.summary: Likelihood ratios multiply prior odds.
lessons.body:
**Odds** compare the chance a hypothesis is true with the chance it is false. A 1% probability is odds of one to 99. Probability and odds express the same belief on different scales.

## Evidence multiplies odds

A **likelihood ratio** compares how likely the observed evidence is under the hypothesis and under its alternative. Evidence more likely under the hypothesis raises its odds; equally likely evidence leaves them unchanged; evidence more likely under the alternative lowers them.

```formula reference
O_post = O_prior × L_ratio
L_ratio = P(E | H) / P(E | ¬H)
where
O_prior: the odds of H before the evidence
O_post: the odds of H after the evidence
L_ratio: the likelihood ratio
H: the hypothesis; ¬H means "H is false" (¬ is "not")
E: the evidence
P(E | H): how likely the evidence is if H is true (| is read "given")
P(E | ¬H): how likely the evidence is if H is false; must be above 0
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: multiply the prior odds by the evidence's likelihood under the hypothesis divided by its likelihood under the alternative.
```

The displayed ratio assumes both hypotheses have positive priors and the evidence has positive probability under the alternative. Multiplying odds is different from multiplying probability. Strong evidence can favour a rare hypothesis without making it the most likely explanation.

## Do repeated results add new information?

After an update, use the posterior as the prior for the next piece of evidence. Conditional independence both when the hypothesis is true and when it is false is sufficient to multiply the individual likelihood ratios unchanged. Without it, calculate each new likelihood ratio conditional on the evidence already seen; do not assume the original ratio still applies.

Copying an alert into a second dashboard does not create a second independent observation. Two tests sharing the same faulty input may repeat the same error. Use the likelihood of the new evidence given what is already known; do not blindly multiply an unchanged ratio again.

Under genuine conditional independence, requiring two positive detectors reduces false positives by requiring both to fire, but also misses real cases whenever either fails to detect them. Improved precision can come at a sensitivity cost.

## Key takeaways
- Likelihood ratios change odds, not probabilities directly.
- Sequential updates must account for previous evidence.
- Conditional independence in both classes permits multiplying the individual likelihood ratios unchanged.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Model feature evidence with naive Bayes
lessons.summary: Conditional independence within each class turns feature likelihoods into a product.
lessons.body:
A **naive Bayes classifier** compares explanations for a set of features. In email, the classes might be spam and **ham**, meaning legitimate email. A word common in spam and uncommon in ham is evidence towards spam; its rate within spam alone is not a posterior probability.

## Combine prior and feature evidence

For each class, start from its prior frequency and combine how typical the observed features are within that class. The naive assumption makes those features conditionally independent given the class, so their likelihood factors multiply. Compare class scores; a common normalising denominator can be omitted when only the winning class matters.

```formula reference
S_c = P(c) × Π_i P(w_i | c)
where
c: a class, here either spam or ham
S_c: the score for category c, proportional to the chance the email is in category c
P(c): the prior, the fraction of training email in category c
w_i: the i-th word of the email
i: a counter running over the words, 1, 2, 3, …
Π_i: the product sign Π, "multiply the following term together for every word i"
P(w_i | c): the probability of token w_i at position i in the class-c token model (| is read "given"), estimated from token counts
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: start with how common the class is, then multiply in how typical each word is of that class.
```

This token model treats word positions as independent draws from a class-specific vocabulary distribution. A document-presence model instead asks whether a word occurs anywhere in the email. Token frequencies and document-presence probabilities are different inputs and cannot be interchanged.

## Useful classification is not calibrated certainty

Two words may occur together in a phrase even within spam messages. Treating them as independent may count overlapping evidence twice and produce overly extreme probabilities. The model can still classify usefully, but a good spam/ham ranking does not demonstrate that a reported probability is calibrated.

When comparing two positive indicators, a second word more characteristic of spam strengthens the spam score under the stated independence model. In practice, check dependence and evaluate predictions on held-out labelled examples.

## Key takeaways
- Compare evidence under competing classes and include their priors.
- Conditional independence simplifies scoring but needs scrutiny.
- Specify whether features describe token occurrences or document presence.

## Further reading
- [Naive Bayes — scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html)
- [A Plan for Spam — Paul Graham](https://www.paulgraham.com/spam.html)

lessons.title: Compute naive Bayes scores with logs and smoothing
lessons.summary: Logs preserve the ranking of positive scores and avoid product underflow.
lessons.body:
Two different problems can make a naive Bayes score collapse: a genuinely zero estimated likelihood, or floating-point underflow from multiplying many small positive numbers. They need different fixes.

## Keep scores usable

**Laplace smoothing** adds one pseudo-count to every token in a fixed finite vocabulary and normalises by the adjusted total. A vocabulary token unseen in one class then has a small positive likelihood rather than vetoing that class. Tokens outside the vocabulary still need an explicit policy.

Taking **log scores** turns products into sums. The logarithm preserves the ordering of positive scores, so the mathematical winning class is unchanged. This avoids product underflow; rounding can still affect very close scores. Logs cannot repair a zero likelihood: the real logarithm of zero is undefined.

## Read the implementation

```python
from math import log

def classify(words, prior, like):
    # Nonempty classes; positive priors.
    # Positive, smoothed likelihoods for
    # each token in a fixed vocabulary.
    words = tuple(words)  # allow generators
    best, best_score = None, float("-inf")
    for c in prior:
        # Logs turn the product into a sum.
        s = log(prior[c])
        for w in words:
            s += log(like[c][w])
        # Keep the largest class score.
        if s > best_score:
            best, best_score = c, s
    return best
```

The inputs must contain a nonempty set of classes, positive priors and a positive likelihood for every supplied token in every class. Converting the words to a tuple lets each class see the same tokens even if the caller supplied a generator. Ties retain the first class encountered.

```formula reference
ln(S_c) = ln(P(c)) + Σ_i ln(P(w_i | c))
P(w | c) = (n_{w,c} + 1) / (N_c + V)
where
ln: the natural logarithm, defined here only for positive scores and probabilities; it turns products into sums and preserves order
S_c: the naive Bayes score for category c
P(c): the prior chance of category c
Σ_i: sigma, "add up the following term for every word i"
w_i, w: a word (token) from the email
P(w | c): the smoothed estimate of the chance of word w in category c (| is read "given")
n_{w,c}: the nonnegative integer count of token w in all training email of category c
N_c: the nonnegative integer total token count in category c’s training email, the sum of its vocabulary token counts
V: the positive integer vocabulary size, the number of distinct tokens in the fixed vocabulary
c: the class, with positive prior probability
i: an index over the finite sequence of email tokens
1: the "add-one" pseudo-count given to every token
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: Add logarithms of positive likelihoods to preserve the score ordering; add-one smoothing gives each token in the fixed vocabulary a positive estimated probability.
```

These formulas document the scoring and smoothing operations. Smoothing prevents vocabulary zeros; logs avoid repeated multiplication. Neither establishes feature independence, repairs a misleading prior or makes the scores calibrated probabilities.

## Key takeaways
- Distinguish unseen-token zeros from numerical underflow.
- Smooth within a defined vocabulary and handle unknown tokens separately.
- Add logs of positive likelihoods while preserving the score ordering.

## Further reading
- [Naive Bayes — scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html)
- [A Plan for Spam — Paul Graham](https://www.paulgraham.com/spam.html)

lessons.title: Turn outcomes into random variables and means
lessons.summary: A random variable is a numerical function of the outcome.
lessons.body:
A **random variable** is a rule that assigns a number to an outcome. The rule is fixed; the outcome is uncertain. Rolling two dice and recording their sum is one rule, while recording whether they match is another.

## Separate outcomes from measurements

A **probability distribution** describes how likely the numerical values are. For a discrete variable, its **probability mass function** gives the probability of each value. In general models the rule must be measurable: events described by its values must belong to the model's permitted collection of events. Finite examples satisfy this automatically.

Counting comparisons in a randomised sort, idle servers after random assignment or bytes transferred all turns uncertain behaviour into numerical quantities we can analyse.

## What a mean predicts

The **expected value** is the probability-weighted average: common values contribute more than rare values. For a discrete finite-mean model, sum each value times its probability. A finite absolute expectation ensures the result is independent of summation order.

```formula reference
E[X] = Σ_x x × P(X = x)
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
E[X]: the expected value of X, the long-run average if the experiment were repeated many times
X: a discrete random variable
x: one of the values X can take
Σ_x: sigma, "add up the following term over every value x"
P(X = x): the probability that X equals x
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: Expectation is the probability-weighted average of possible numerical values, when the finite absolute expectation exists.
```

A fair six-sided die has expected value 3.5 even though no roll shows 3.5. The mean describes averaging across repetitions, not a promised or most likely individual outcome.

Under independent identically distributed repetitions with finite absolute expectation, sample averages converge to the expectation by the **law of large numbers**. This does not guarantee that each additional observation improves an estimate. Some distributions have no finite expectation, so check that the mean being discussed exists.

## Key takeaways
- A random variable numerically describes an uncertain outcome.
- Expectation weights values by their probabilities.
- The mean need not be an observable value or a single-run prediction.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Understand the expected wait for success
lessons.summary: Independent constant-probability attempts restart after a failure.
lessons.body:
An expected retry count describes average load, not a deadline. Even when success has a finite expected wait, a particular request can need many more attempts.

## A fresh chance after every failure

Assume attempts are independent and each has the same positive success probability. Count all attempts up to and including the first success. This is the **geometric distribution**.

After a failed attempt, the future process has the same distribution as it had initially. You have spent one attempt, but have made no progress towards a success being “due”. A larger success probability shortens the expected wait; halving it doubles the mean attempt count.

```formula reference
E[T] = 1 / p
where
T: the number of attempts up to and including the first success
E[T]: the expected (long-run average) number of attempts
p: the fixed success probability for an independent attempt, greater than zero and at most one
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: With independent attempts and a constant positive success chance, the mean total attempts through success is the reciprocal of that chance.
```

For a success chance of one in five, the mean is five total attempts. That includes the successful attempt, so failures-only counts are one smaller. A run can still end on its first attempt or continue far beyond five.

## Why the mean is finite

Each extra failure multiplies the probability of still waiting by the same factor below one. The resulting geometric tail has a finite sum, which justifies the finite mean. At success probability one, the first attempt always succeeds; at zero, this proper finite-mean model does not apply.

In a real overloaded service, attempts may share a persistent cause and retries may worsen the overload. The constant independent chance is an assumption to test, not a reason to retry without a limit or delay.

## Key takeaways
- Count the successful attempt when interpreting geometric waiting time.
- A finite expectation does not impose a maximum wait.
- Retry-load estimates depend on constant independent success chances.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Separate spread from linearity
lessons.summary: Variance measures squared spread; standard deviation uses the original units.
lessons.body:
Two services can have the same mean latency but very different consistency. **Variance** measures average squared distance from the mean; **standard deviation** is its square root and uses the original units. Latency variance is in squared time units, while latency standard deviation is a time.

## Spread differs from uncertainty about a mean

Variance describes the distribution of individual values. A finite second moment, meaning a finite expected square, ensures finite variance. The mean alone does not tell you whether delays are consistent or highly variable.

```formula reference
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)^2]
Var(X) = E[X^2] − μ^2
σ = √(Var(X))
where
X: a random variable
μ: mu, the mean of X, the same as E[X]
E[ ]: expected value, the probability-weighted average of whatever is inside the brackets
E[X^2]: the expectation of the square of X, not the square of its expectation
Var(X): the variance of X, in the units of X squared
σ: sigma, the standard deviation of X, in the same units as X
√: the square root
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
Moments: variables in these variance or covariance expressions have finite second moments
In words: variance is the average squared distance from the mean, which also equals the mean of the square minus the square of the mean; its square root is the standard deviation.
```

## Means add even when values move together

For variables with finite absolute expectations, **linearity of expectation** says the expected total is the sum of the expected parts. Scaling or shifting a quantity scales or shifts its expectation too.

```formula essential
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]
E[a × X + b] = a × E[X] + b
where
X, Y: any two random variables, dependent or not
E[ ]: expected value
a, b: fixed numbers (constants), not random
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: the average of a sum is the sum of the averages, and scaling or shifting a variable scales or shifts its average the same way.
```

No independence is needed. Correlated request counts can still be added to obtain the expected total. This lets us count many small events without deriving the full distribution of their total.

## Do not extend linearity to everything

Variances do not generally add: positive covariance adds spread to a sum, while negative covariance can reduce it. With finite second moments, zero covariance makes the variance of a sum equal the sum of variances and makes the mean of a product equal the product of means. Independence implies zero covariance in this setting; the converse need not hold.

Likewise, averaging after squaring is not generally the same as squaring the average. They agree only when the variable is constant with probability one. For non-linear transformations, reason about the transformed outcomes before taking their average.

## Key takeaways
- Standard deviation uses the original units; variance uses squared units.
- Finite means add regardless of dependence.
- Products, variances and non-linear transformations need separate reasoning.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Count fixed points with indicators
lessons.summary: Each indicator has expectation equal to its event probability.
lessons.body:
To find an expected count, ask a small yes/no question for each item. An **indicator variable** is one when its event happens and zero otherwise. Its mean is the event's probability.

## Build a count from simple pieces

Give every trial an indicator for success. Adding the indicators gives the total successes. **Linearity of expectation** then adds their probabilities to obtain the expected count, even when the events are dependent.

Ten flips each with marginal head probability 0.3 have expected total three heads. Independence would be needed to call the full count binomial, but is unnecessary for this mean.

## Random returns in a cloakroom

A cloakroom returns a positive number of coats in uniformly random order. Each owner has the same chance of receiving any coat, so their own coat is one possibility among the whole group. Add one match indicator per owner: there is one match on average, regardless of group size.

This is an expectation, not a guarantee of one match in each shuffle. The matches are dependent: if everyone but the final owner receives the correct coat, the final owner must too. That does not invalidate linearity. A match is called a **fixed point** of the permutation.

```python
import random

def fixed_points(n):
    p = list(range(n))
    # Assign each owner a shuffled item.
    random.shuffle(p)
    return sum(p[i] == i for i in range(n))

t = 100_000
print(sum(fixed_points(50)
          for _ in range(t)) / t)  # ~1.0
```

This simulation averages match counts from repeated random shuffles. It should approach one, with variation between runs. The explanation using indicators is what establishes the model expectation.

## Key takeaways
- A count is a sum of yes/no indicators.
- Add individual probabilities to obtain an expected count.
- Dependence affects the distribution without preventing linearity.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Count empty servers and inversions
lessons.summary: Random assignment leaves many servers idle even with one job per server on average.
lessons.body:
An average of one job per server does not mean each server receives one job. Independent uniform assignment allows repeats, leaving some servers idle while others receive several jobs.

## Ask one question per server

For a fixed server to be idle, every job must miss it. Under independent assignments those avoidance probabilities multiply. Add one empty-server indicator per server to obtain the expected number idle.

With 100 jobs independently assigned to 100 equally likely servers, about 37 servers are idle on average. The total work still averages one job per server; that average says nothing about the fullest server. Sampling two candidate servers and choosing the less loaded can improve balance under an appropriate sequential allocation model with current load information.

## Ask one question per pair

An **inversion** is a pair of positions where the earlier value exceeds the later value. In a uniformly random permutation of distinct values, each pair is equally likely to be in either order. Half the pairs are therefore inverted on average.

Adjacent-swap insertion sort removes one inversion per swap; the usual shifting implementation makes one rightward shift per inversion. Because the number of pairs grows quadratically with array length, so does average insertion-sort work on these random permutations. Nearly sorted inputs with few inversions behave differently.

## Transfer the method to hashing

Keys assigned independently to uniform buckets behave like jobs assigned to servers. A specified bucket's expected occupancy, the number of empty buckets and the number of colliding key pairs are three different quantities.

A bucket with three keys contains three colliding pairs, not one. Pair counts can exceed bucket counts. The maximum occupancy is not a sum of per-bucket occupancies, so linearity does not directly give its expectation.

## Key takeaways
- Average occupancy does not describe imbalance or the maximum.
- Choose indicators for the quantity actually being counted.
- Pairs explain both inversions and collisions.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Find harmonic expectations for records and coverage
lessons.summary: A record at a given position has reciprocal-position probability.
lessons.body:
Random sampling makes discovery easy at first and harder later. Two common examples are finding a new record while scanning values and visiting every shard by random probing.

## Records become less frequent

```python
def scan(a):
    best = float("-inf")
    updates = 0
    for x in a:
        # Count only new record values.
        if x > best:
            best = x
            updates += 1
    return updates
```

This function counts new running maxima, not comparisons. It examines every item even when no new record occurs.

For a uniformly random permutation of distinct finite values, each of the first few positions is equally likely to contain their largest value. The first position always sets a record; later positions have progressively smaller record chances. Adding one indicator per position gives a **harmonic number**, which grows logarithmically with input length.

This describes the average number of record updates. Ascending input updates every time; descending input updates only at the start. Neither ordering is representative of all uniform permutations.

## Complete coverage gets progressively harder

In the **coupon collector** model, each request independently selects one of a fixed positive number of equally likely shards, with replacement. Early requests often find a new shard. Near the end, most requests revisit known shards.

Break the process into stages. Within a stage, the set of missing shards is fixed, so the wait for a new one is geometric. As that set shrinks, the chance of progress falls and the expected stage wait rises. Add the stage means to find the expected total; it grows like shard count times its logarithm.

The final missing shard alone takes one shard-count's worth of requests on average. One request per shard therefore does not imply complete coverage. If coverage is required and the list is known, deliberately visiting each shard avoids this random repetition.

## Key takeaways
- Record updates are rarer later, although the scan still examines every item.
- Random coverage slows as fewer unseen targets remain.
- Uniform sampling with replacement is different from a planned traversal.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Bound tails from mean and variance
lessons.summary: Markov needs a nonnegative variable and a positive threshold.
lessons.body:
A mean does not determine how often extreme values occur, but it can constrain them. A **tail bound** gives a limit, not the exact tail probability.

## A budget argument for nonnegative quantities

**Markov’s inequality** applies to a nonnegative variable with known finite mean and a positive threshold. Every observation above the threshold consumes at least that much of the average's total budget. Too many such observations would force the mean higher.

```formula reference
P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
X: a random variable that is never negative, with a finite mean
a: any positive threshold in the same units as X
P(X ≥ a): the probability that X is at least a
E[X]: the expected value (mean) of X
≥: greater than or equal to
≤: less than or equal to
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: For a nonnegative quantity, divide its finite mean by a positive threshold to bound the probability of reaching or exceeding that threshold.
```

For nonnegative latency with mean 20 milliseconds, at most 20% can be at least 100 milliseconds. That bound could be attained by putting 20% exactly at the threshold and the rest at zero. Another distribution with the same mean could have no observations at that threshold. The mean alone cannot distinguish them.

## Variance adds information about deviations

**Chebyshev’s inequality** bounds deviations on either side of the mean using finite variance. At two standard deviations, at most one-quarter of the probability can lie that far or farther from the mean; the usual form assumes a positive standard deviation. A zero-variance variable is constant with probability one and can be treated separately.

Neither inequality requires a normal distribution. Chebyshev is not automatically tighter than every Markov bound: they use different information and may describe different events. Stronger assumptions about a distribution can yield tighter bounds, but must be justified.

## Key takeaways
- An upper bound is not an estimated or exact tail probability.
- Markov requires nonnegativity and a finite mean.
- Chebyshev uses variance without assuming a bell curve.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Average transfer times rather than rates
lessons.summary: Compute the duration in each outcome before averaging.
lessons.body:
A fast transfer cannot cancel a slow transfer simply because their speeds average neatly. First decide what you are averaging: speed at a moment, speed per transfer, or the duration of a fixed job.

## Average the quantity you need

Each 100-megabyte download independently chooses either 10 or 90 megabytes per second with equal probability and keeps that speed throughout. Ignore overhead. The slow download lasts 10 seconds and the fast one about 1.11 seconds, giving a mean duration about 5.56 seconds.

The mean of the two chosen speeds is 50 megabytes per second. Dividing the file size by that mean gives two seconds, which does not describe the expected duration. The reciprocal relationship between speed and time is non-linear: calculate time in each outcome before averaging.

## Why slow transfers matter so much

Halving a speed doubles the time for the same file. A very slow possibility can therefore add substantial waiting time, even when a fast possibility makes the average speed look attractive. For positive speeds and finite relevant expectations, **Jensen’s inequality** formalises why dividing by the expected speed underestimates or equals the expected duration.

A single transfer spending equal amounts of time at the two rates is a different model. Likewise, averaging throughput over elapsed time weights observations differently from averaging one chosen speed per fixed-size transfer. State the sampling unit before combining rates.

## Key takeaways
- Convert each outcome to the required quantity before averaging.
- Per-transfer and per-time rate averages answer different questions.
- Non-linear transformations do not generally commute with expectation.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Model fixed trials with the binomial
lessons.summary: A binomial count needs independent trials with one fixed probability.
lessons.body:
A distribution is useful when its assumptions describe the process. Start by asking what you count and when you stop, rather than choosing a familiar formula.

## Fixed trials, count the successes

A **Bernoulli trial** has two outcomes, conventionally called success and failure. “Success” is just the counted outcome: a failed disk can be a success for a failure-count model.

A **binomial distribution** counts successes in a fixed number of mutually independent trials with the same success probability. Independent disks with one common annual failure chance fit this model if you count failed original disks. Shared power failures or different disk risks violate its assumptions.

## Count arrangements as well as one sequence

For exactly three heads in five coin flips, one arrangement is heads-heads-heads-tails-tails. Other arrangements have the same count. The binomial probability includes every such arrangement, not just the displayed sequence. For fair independent flips, sequences are equally likely; the possible head counts are not.

```formula reference
X ~ Bin(n, p)
P(X = k) = C(n, k) × p^k × (1 − p)^{n − k}
C(n, k) = n! / (k! × (n − k)!)
E[X] = n × p
Var(X) = n × p × (1 − p)
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
X: the number of successes, a whole number from 0 to n
~: "is distributed as", "has the distribution"
Bin(n, p): the binomial distribution with n trials and success probability p
n: the nonnegative integer number of trials
p: the common trial success probability, between 0 and 1; use the displayed mass formula away from the endpoints
k: a particular number of successes we ask about, 0 to n
P(X = k): the probability of exactly k successes
C(n, k): "n choose k", the number of ways to pick which k of the n trials succeed
!: factorial; n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1, and 0! = 1
p^k: k copies of p multiplied together, the chance that k chosen trials all succeed
(1 − p)^{n − k}: the chance that the other n − k trials all fail
E[X]: the expected (mean) number of successes
Var(X): the variance of the number of successes
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
Moments: variables in these variance or covariance expressions have finite second moments
In words: multiply the number of arrangements with the requested success count by the probability of one arrangement. The expected count is the trial count times the common success probability.
```

The endpoint cases are simple: success probability zero produces no successes; probability one produces success on every trial. Treat them directly rather than evaluating ambiguous powers in the general mass formula.

## Accumulating small risks

For a transfer to lose no packets, every packet must survive. Under independent loss with a fixed nonzero rate, a longer transfer has more opportunities for loss, even though each packet's risk stays unchanged. An expected loss count of one does not guarantee exactly one loss.

A fixed count of trials differs from continuing until the first success, which calls for a geometric waiting-time model. Bursty losses need a dependence model rather than an automatic binomial assumption.

## Key takeaways
- Binomial counts need fixed trials, independence and one common success probability.
- Include every arrangement giving the requested count.
- A small per-trial risk can accumulate across many trials.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Apply binomial counts to fleets and quorums
lessons.summary: Disk counts refer to the original fleet, not replacements.
lessons.body:
A model of failed components answers a narrower question than “will the service work?” Specify the population, time window and failure condition before using a binomial count.

## Count an original fleet

Suppose every original disk has the same annual failure probability and the failures are independent. The number of those disks that fail during the year is binomial. It does not count failures of replacements installed during the year: those add new exposures outside the original set of trials.

The expected failure count is useful for average demand, but stocking exactly that many spares does not control shortage risk. A policy also needs a tolerated shortage probability and replenishment time. Shared manufacturing defects or infrastructure can make a simple independent model optimistic.

## Translate quorum rules into count events

A fixed five-node **majority quorum** needs three reachable cooperating members. Considering node downtime alone, up to two nodes can be down while a majority remains; three or more down prevents one.

Under identical independent downtime chances at a sampled instant, use the binomial tail covering three, four and five failed nodes. Counting one specific group of three misses the other groups that can fail. Counting at least one failure asks about a different event that the cluster can tolerate.

Even an accurate node-downtime estimate is not total service unavailability. Network partitions, elections, recovery and routing may stop service while enough nodes are technically up. Turning a sampled-instant probability into expected annual downtime also assumes appropriate stable marginal probabilities.

## Key takeaways
- State whether the population includes replacement components.
- Mean demand alone does not set a spare-stock policy.
- Quorum loss depends on a threshold count and still omits other service failure causes.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Model geometric waits and memorylessness
lessons.summary: The geometric distribution counts through the first success.
lessons.body:
A **geometric distribution** models the number of independent constant-probability trials up to and including the first success. It answers a waiting question, not a count within a fixed batch.

## A run of failures does not make success due

When the success probability is strictly between zero and one and attempts are independent, knowing that several attempts failed leaves the future trial distribution unchanged. The remaining wait has the same distribution as the original wait. This is **memorylessness**.

The expected further wait is therefore unchanged after any possible failure streak. Total attempts so far still increase: memorylessness concerns what remains, not erasing the cost already paid. A long wait remains possible even when the expected wait is short.

```formula reference
P(T = k) = (1 − p)^{k − 1} × p
E[T] = 1 / p
Var(T) = (1 − p) / p^2
P(T > k) = (1 − p)^k
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
T: the number of trials up to and including the first success
k: a particular trial count, 1, 2, 3, …
p: the fixed success probability, strictly between 0 and 1 for the displayed mass formula; success probability one is the deterministic case described below
(1 − p)^{k − 1}: the chance the first k − 1 trials all fail
P(T = k): the probability that the first success is on trial k
E[T]: the expected number of trials
Var(T): the variance of the number of trials
p^2: p multiplied by itself
P(T > k): the probability of still having no success after k trials
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
Moments: variables in these variance or covariance expressions have finite second moments
In words: a first success on a chosen attempt requires every earlier attempt to fail. The mean wait is the reciprocal of the success chance; each extra failure multiplies the remaining tail probability by the fixed failure chance.
```

At success probability one, the first attempt succeeds with certainty. A failure streak is then impossible and cannot be used as an ordinary conditioning event. Success probability zero gives no eventual success and falls outside this proper geometric model.

## Check whether the real process remembers

After several failed requests, a persistent outage may be more plausible than it was before. That is evidence against treating every attempt as an independent draw with a fixed success chance. Retries can also add load and change the chance of recovery.

Backoff can reduce retry pressure, but its effect requires a system model. Open-addressing hash probes also generally do not behave like independent draws with replacement, so a geometric model is a simplification rather than a universal probing law.

## Key takeaways
- Memorylessness describes the remaining wait under specific assumptions.
- Past effort does not make success due in an independent fixed-probability model.
- Persistent causes or changing conditions invalidate that simple interpretation.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Model Poisson counts and rare-trial approximations
lessons.summary: A Poisson parameter is an expected count in a specified window.
lessons.body:
A **Poisson distribution** describes a nonnegative whole-number count. Its parameter is the expected count in a specified window, so “three per hour” and “three per minute” cannot be substituted without changing the window.

## Where the model comes from

An exact example is the count during a fixed window of a homogeneous **Poisson process**: a process with constant intensity and independent increments. A suitable collection of many independent rare opportunities can also have an approximately Poisson count.

An average of three events per hour does not mean three arrive every hour. Quiet windows and bursts are possible even in a constant-rate model. Increasing the window's expected count reduces its chance of being empty.

```formula reference
P(X = k) = (λ^k e^{−λ}) / k!
E[X] = λ
Var(X) = λ
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
X: the number of events in the window (0, 1, 2, …)
k: a nonnegative integer count we ask about
λ: lambda, the positive expected count in the window for the displayed mass formula; the zero-mean case is described below
P(X = k): the probability of exactly k events
e: Euler's number, about 2.718, the base of natural logarithms; e^{−λ} is the chance of no events at all
λ^k: λ multiplied by itself k times
!: factorial; k! = k × (k − 1) × … × 1, and 0! = 1
E[X]: the expected count
Var(X): the variance of the count
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
Moments: variables in these variance or covariance expressions have finite second moments
In words: within a Poisson model, the expected count determines every count probability; it also equals the count variance.
```

At expected count zero, the count is always zero. This is a separate deterministic endpoint of the model.

## Test a proposed approximation

A binomial count can be approximated by a Poisson count when there are many trials with small individual success probabilities. Use the same expected count. Fair coin tosses do not have rare successes, so this is not generally a good approximation to their head count.

The Poisson mean equals its variance. Substantially larger observed count variance, called **overdispersion**, is a warning: bursts, varying intensity or mixed populations may invalidate a single Poisson model. Sample estimates vary, and mean–variance agreement alone does not establish the distribution.

Retries until success are a waiting-time question, not events per window. Always specify what the random quantity counts before selecting a distribution.

## Key takeaways
- Attach an explicit window to a Poisson expected count.
- Independent rare trials can motivate an approximation.
- A stable average alone does not establish a Poisson process.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Interpret Poisson tails and combine streams
lessons.summary: Arrival-count exceedance is different from queueing delay or exceeding queue capacity.
lessons.body:
A service whose average arrivals are below capacity can still receive busy windows. To estimate that risk, look at the arrival-count tail, while keeping it separate from actual queueing behaviour.

## Interpret a tail calculation

Suppose arrivals follow a homogeneous Poisson process averaging five per second. The code computes the chance of ten or more arrivals in a one-second window by subtracting the probabilities of zero through nine from one.

```python
from math import exp, factorial

def poisson_pmf(k, lam):
    return lam**k * exp(-lam) / factorial(k)

lam = 5
# Sum counts within the nine-request limit.
p_ok = sum(poisson_pmf(k, lam)
           for k in range(10))
print(round(1 - p_ok, 4))  # 0.0318
```

The result is about 3.18%. It describes arrival-count exceedance of a nine-request threshold. It is not automatically the chance of a full queue or high latency: those also depend on existing backlog, buffering and service times. A higher threshold reduces this count-tail probability without removing all uncertainty.

The direct calculation is suitable for this small example. Large arguments or tiny tails need numerical methods that stay within floating-point range and avoid cancellation; a distribution library's survival function is usually preferable to subtracting a nearly-one cumulative probability.

## Combining and selecting streams

**Poisson superposition** says independent Poisson streams combine into another Poisson stream whose rates add. Independent regions at two and three requests per second produce five per second together. A quiet combined window requires both regions to be quiet; averaging their quiet probabilities is wrong.

**Poisson thinning** independently keeps each event with a fixed probability, producing another Poisson stream with a reduced rate. A label based on a shared burst or changing state does not meet that assumption.

For a homogeneous Poisson process with positive rate, **inter-arrival times** follow an exponential distribution. A larger rate means a shorter average gap.

## Key takeaways
- A count exceeding a threshold does not directly measure queue failure.
- Superposition needs independent Poisson streams.
- Thinning needs independent fixed-probability selection.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Read normal probabilities using z-scores
lessons.summary: A normal model is specified by its mean and positive standard deviation.
lessons.body:
A **normal distribution** is a continuous symmetric bell curve. Its mean locates the centre and its positive standard deviation sets the spread. A larger spread makes the same absolute distance from the centre less unusual.

## Standardise distance

A **z-score** describes how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean. Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. Positive values are above the mean; negative ones are below. This comparison needs a finite positive standard deviation, but computing a z-score does not itself make data normal.

```formula reference
z = (x − μ) / σ
where
z: the z-score of x, with no units
x: one particular value
μ: mu, the mean
σ: sigma, the positive standard deviation, in the same units as the observations
In words: Subtract the mean and divide by the positive standard deviation to express distance from the centre in units of spread.
```

Under a normal model, roughly 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. These are two-sided bands. The upper edge of the three-standard-deviation band is about the 99.865th percentile, because only half the remaining probability lies above it.

## Use the model, not just the scale

For a normal response-size model with mean 500 kilobytes and standard deviation 50 kilobytes, 600 kilobytes is two standard deviations above the mean. If spread doubles while the mean stays fixed, that same response is less unusual.

A normal law allows all real values. For a nonnegative quantity it can only be an approximation, and its negative tail may be unacceptable. A z-score alone does not give a tail probability for an arbitrary distribution; use the distributional model or measured observations.

## Key takeaways
- Mean and standard deviation control location and spread in a normal model.
- Z-scores compare distance on a common scale.
- Normal percentage bands are two-sided and are not universal rules.

## Further reading
- [Normal distribution — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm)

lessons.title: Check a normal approximation and choose a model
lessons.summary: The iid finite-variance CLT is a limiting statement.
lessons.body:
Averages can become more stable and more nearly bell-shaped than individual observations. The **central limit theorem (CLT)** explains one important case, but it is not permission to treat every data set as normal.

## What approaches a normal distribution?

For independent identically distributed observations with finite nonzero variance, the centred and scaled sum, or equivalently the centred and scaled average, converges in distribution to a standard normal as the sample grows. This is a limiting statement; there is no universal sample size that guarantees accurate tail estimates.

The original observations do not thereby become normal. For independent copies with the same variance, the sum's standard deviation grows with the square root of the count, while the average's standard deviation shrinks with that square root. Quadrupling observations halves the average's standard deviation.

## Choose a model from the process

| Quantity | Candidate model |
|---|---|
| Success count in fixed independent equal-probability trials | Binomial |
| Independent equal-probability trials until success | Geometric |
| Count in a homogeneous Poisson-process window | Poisson |
| Standardised average meeting CLT assumptions | Approximate normal |

A binomial normal approximation needs enough expected successes and failures. A Poisson normal approximation improves as its mean grows. A **continuity correction** treats whole-number counts as intervals extending half a unit on either side, but does not repair invalid assumptions.

## Inspect latency tails directly

Mean and standard deviation do not determine high percentiles. Latency can be skewed or multimodal; nonnegativity alone proves neither skewness nor a heavy tail. A normal approximation may fit central observations while misrepresenting rare delays that matter to an SLO.

Use enough observations or an appropriate histogram to estimate the relevant tail and its uncertainty. Dependence, changing traffic and rare extreme values all require attention before trusting an approximation.

## Key takeaways
- The CLT concerns standardised sums or averages under stated assumptions.
- Large samples do not provide a universal tail-accuracy guarantee.
- Choose models by process and check the predictions that matter.

## Further reading
- [Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf)

lessons.title: Distinguish randomised algorithm guarantees
lessons.summary: Las Vegas correctness is certain while runtime can vary.
lessons.body:
When an algorithm uses randomness, ask which part of its promise is uncertain: the answer, the amount of work, or both. An average running time is different from a limit on every execution.

## Two kinds of guarantee

A **Las Vegas algorithm** produces a correct answer when it returns; its running time depends on random choices. Quicksort with fresh uniform pivots always sorts its distinct-key input correctly, but an unlucky sequence can still cause quadratic work.

A **Monte Carlo algorithm** has a controlled running-time budget but may return an incorrect answer. The randomised Miller–Rabin primality test can label a composite input “probably prime”. For a fixed odd composite and a uniformly chosen base in the required range, at most one-quarter of bases fool a round.

## What repetition buys

For the same fixed composite to fool several independent rounds, every round must accept it. Independence lets their error bounds multiply. More rounds reduce the fixed-input error bound; reusing the same random base does not supply fresh independent evidence.

```formula reference
P(F) ≤ (1/4)^k
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
F: the event "a fixed odd composite input passes all k rounds"
k: the positive integer number of independent Miller–Rabin rounds
1/4: the most a single round can be fooled, when its base is chosen uniformly at random
P(F): the probability of F
≤: less than or equal to
In words: Each independent uniformly sampled round reduces the stated fixed-composite acceptance bound by a factor of four.
```

The bound concerns acceptance conditional on a fixed composite input. It is not the posterior probability that a candidate is composite after acceptance; that also depends on how candidates were selected. The distinction is the same confusion about the direction of conditioning encountered with alert detectors.

Choose the number of rounds from the acceptable error bound and threat model, using a trusted implementation. Do not substitute predictable random choices for the stated uniform independent sampling assumption.

## Key takeaways
- Las Vegas correctness and random runtime are separate properties.
- Independent repetition can reduce a Monte Carlo error bound.
- A fixed-input error bound is not automatically a posterior probability.

## Further reading
- [Miller–Rabin error bounds — Handbook of Applied Cryptography, chapter 4](https://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/hac/about/chap4.pdf)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/)

lessons.title: Analyse hashing load and adversarial keys
lessons.summary: Expected bucket occupancy is the load factor under uniform hashing.
lessons.body:
A hash table's expected performance depends on how keys reach buckets. **Simple uniform hashing** assumes each key independently chooses a uniformly random bucket. Real implementations and adversarial inputs need separate scrutiny.

## Average occupancy is not the worst bucket

The **load factor** is stored keys divided by buckets. Under the uniform model, it is the expected occupancy of a specified bucket. In a **chained hash table**, an unsuccessful lookup scans its selected bucket; with bounded-cost hashing and comparisons, keeping the load factor bounded keeps expected lookup cost bounded.

Collisions are ordinary. More keys create more pairs that can collide, even when each bucket's expected occupancy looks small. The mean occupancy does not guarantee short chains in every bucket.

**Open addressing** stores keys directly in slots and probes alternatives after a collision. As the table fills, searches for an empty slot become harder. Linear probing can form long runs of occupied slots, so a high load factor hurts more than a simple occupancy average suggests.

## Challenge the input model

An attacker able to construct colliding keys can defeat uniform-model expectations. In a list-backed bucket, each insertion may scan existing keys; a large batch then causes quadratic total work, where input size means the number of supplied keys.

Resizing may separate keys that only shared a bucket index, but it cannot separate identical full hash values under the same hash function. An appropriate secret keyed hash makes precomputed attacks harder. Input limits still matter, as do key types, key handling and adaptive attackers.

Python randomises hashes for covered string and byte keys by default; configuration and other key types need checking. Do not infer that every object is protected merely because a process has a hash seed.

## Key takeaways
- Uniform expected occupancy is not a maximum-load guarantee.
- High occupancy particularly hurts probing schemes.
- Untrusted keys require defences beyond an average-case model.

## Further reading
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/)
