lessons.title: Understand the birthday collision bound
lessons.summary: The no-collision calculation multiplies successive avoidance probabilities.
lessons.body:
A collision asks whether any pair matches. That creates far more opportunities than asking whether one new item matches a particular existing item.

## Count opportunities in pairs

Under independent uniform birthdays over 365 days, 23 people already give just over a 50% chance of a shared birthday. The surprise comes from all the pairs in the group, not from filling half the calendar.

To find the exact model probability, consider the complement: every birthday differs. Each new person must avoid all previously used days. Multiply those successive avoidance chances, then subtract from one. The avoidance chance changes as more dates are used.

## How the risk grows

For independent uniform draws from a large space, collisions become likely when the number of draws is around the square root of the space size. Doubling a small population roughly quadruples its pair count and hence its small collision risk.

```formula reference
P(C) ≈ 1 − e^{−(n(n − 1)) / (2m)}
n_{1/2} ≈ √(2 × ln(2) × m)
where
C: the event "at least two draws collide (are equal)"
n: the nonnegative integer number of independent uniform draws (people, IDs, hashes)
m: the positive integer number of equally likely values (365 days, 2^32 IDs, …)
e: Euler's number, about 2.718; each factor 1 − i/m is close to e^{−i/m} when i is small next to m
n_{1/2}: the number of draws at which a collision becomes a 50% chance
ln(2): the natural logarithm of 2, about 0.693
√: the square root
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
≈: approximately equal to
In words: Under independent uniform sampling from a large space, collision probability becomes substantial around the square root of the space size.
```

This approximation is useful near the square-root scale for large spaces. Real birthdays need not be independent or uniform; poor random ID generation can similarly concentrate outcomes and increase risk relative to the ideal model.

The expected number of matching pairs and the probability of any match are different. A three-person shared birthday contributes three pairs. An expected pair count can exceed one while a probability cannot.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: introductions at a party
> Every new guest can be introduced to everyone already present.
>
> **How it maps:** Each arrival adds several new pairs, just as each new random ID creates collision opportunities with all previous IDs.
>
> **Where it stops:** An introduction is deliberate; a collision occurs only when a pair's independently generated values match under the model.

## Key takeaways
- Any-pair risk grows much faster than one-target risk.
- The complement tracks successive avoidance chances.
- Matching-pair expectation is not a collision probability.

## Further reading
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/)

lessons.title: Choose ID and hash lengths using birthday risk
lessons.summary: Independent random IDs need enough space for pairwise collision risk.
lessons.body:
Choose a random identifier space from the expected population and acceptable collision risk. A large-looking range is not enough: every new ID can collide with every earlier ID.

## Population and space size both matter

Under independent uniform generation and small collision risk, doubling the issued population roughly quadruples the risk. Adding one random bit doubles the space and roughly halves that risk. These are planning approximations, not guarantees of uniqueness.

```formula reference
P(C) ≈ n^2 / (2 × m)
where
C: the event "at least one collision"
n: the integer number of independent uniform items (IDs), large enough to approximate the pair count using its squared leading term
m: the positive integer number of possible values; 2^32 ≈ 4.29 billion for a 32-bit ID
n^2: n multiplied by itself
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
≈: approximately equal to (good while the result is well below 1)
In words: For many independent uniform IDs while collision risk is small, risk is approximately proportional to the square of the population and inversely proportional to the space size.
```

A 32-bit random ID has billions of possible values, yet issuing 10,000 carries roughly a 1.2% chance of some collision under this model. If collisions are unacceptable, detect duplicates and retry or use a coordinated allocation scheme as appropriate.

A version 4 UUID is 128 bits overall, including 122 random bits and fixed version and variant fields. The random space is enormous, but generation quality and the number issued still matter. Fixed formatting bits add no randomness.

## Accidental uniqueness and attack resistance differ

A classical generic **birthday attack** searches for any two inputs with the same ideal hash. It needs work on the order of the square root of the output-space size. Thus an ideal 128-bit hash has about 64-bit generic collision resistance.

A **preimage attack** instead targets one already specified output, a different and generically harder task. Cryptanalytic weaknesses can also beat generic bounds; output length alone does not make a hash secure. MD5 and SHA-1 have demonstrated collision weaknesses beyond the birthday bound.

## Key takeaways
- Size IDs for all-pairs risk and the expected population.
- Random formatting does not guarantee uniqueness.
- Distinguish generic collision search, preimage search and algorithm-specific weaknesses.

lessons.title: Prove expected quicksort comparisons
lessons.summary: A pair is compared when an endpoint is the first pivot in its rank interval.
lessons.body:
Random pivots protect quicksort's expected comparison count against a fixed bad input order. They do not remove unlucky executions. The reason becomes clear by following one pair of values.

## Specify the comparison model

Assume distinct totally ordered keys, fresh independent uniform pivots, and one comparison between each pivot and every other element in its partition. The input is fixed independently of those choices.

A first-element pivot on sorted input repeatedly removes only one element, giving quadratic work. A uniform pivot can occupy any rank, so sorted input has the same comparison-count distribution as any other fixed ordering of distinct keys.

## Follow a pair through the partitions

Consider two values and all values between them in sorted order. Pivots outside this interval leave the pair together. The first pivot chosen from within the interval determines whether they ever meet:

- An endpoint pivot is compared with the other endpoint.
- An interior pivot separates the endpoints into different recursive calls, so they never meet.

```formula essential
P(X_ij = 1) = 2 / (j − i + 1)
where
z_1 < z_2 < … < z_n: the n elements in sorted order
i, j: integer ranks from one through n, with i < j; pivots are fresh independent uniform choices
X_ij: the indicator that z_i and z_j are ever compared: 1 if so, 0 if not
j − i + 1: the number of elements in the block from z_i to z_j
2: the two "good" first pivots, z_i or z_j
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: two elements are compared only if one of them is the first pivot picked from the block between them, a chance of 2 divided by the number of elements in the block.
```

Every element in the interval is equally likely to be that first pivot. There are exactly two favourable endpoints. Nearby ranks are therefore more likely to be compared than distant ranks.

## Turn pairs into total work

Each pair is compared at most once because a pivot is excluded from later recursive calls. Give each pair an indicator and add its comparison probability. Linearity requires no independence between the indicators.

```formula reference
E[Q] = Σ_{i<j} 2 / (j − i + 1)
E[Q] = 2 × (n + 1) × H_n − 4 × n
E[Q] ≈ 2 × n × ln(n)
where
Q: the total number of comparisons
E[Q]: its expected value
n: the positive integer number of distinct totally ordered elements, with fresh independent uniform pivots and one comparison per pivot-other-element pair
i, j: integer ranks from one through n, with i less than j
Σ_{i<j}: sigma, "add up over every pair with i less than j"
H_n: the n-th harmonic number, 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n (base e ≈ 2.718)
≈: approximately equal to (for large n)
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: nearby ranks are compared more often than distant ranks. Adding every pair's comparison probability gives an expected total growing as input length times its logarithm.
```

The expected count grows as input length times its logarithm. A particular pivot sequence can still give quadratic work. Duplicates, adaptive comparisons or predictable pivot choices need their own analysis rather than inheriting this guarantee automatically.

## Key takeaways
- The first pivot within a rank interval decides whether its endpoints meet.
- Pair indicators turn local probabilities into expected total work.
- The expectation is over pivots for every fixed distinct-key input.

lessons.title: Check quicksort runtime and production safeguards
lessons.summary: A sampled comparison count is one draw, rather than proof of the mean.
lessons.body:
A measured quicksort execution is one draw from a runtime distribution. Repeating it can check an expected-comparison prediction, but one fast run cannot establish either the mean or a worst-case guarantee.

## Count the work actually performed

```python
import random

def qs(a):
    # Distinct keys with a total order.
    # Count actual pivot comparisons.
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return 0
    # Every element can be the next pivot.
    i = random.randrange(len(a))
    p = a[i]
    lo, hi = [], []
    for j, x in enumerate(a):
        # Skip the pivot itself.
        if j == i:
            continue
        if x < p:
            lo.append(x)
        else:
            hi.append(x)
    # Count this partition and both sides.
    return (len(a) - 1) + qs(lo) + qs(hi)

print(qs(list(range(1000))))
# One run; the mean is about 10,986.
```

This function counts pivot comparisons; it does not return the sorted array. It assumes distinct keys with a total order. Every partition compares its pivot once with each other element, then adds the two recursive counts.

For 1,000 distinct keys and fresh independent uniform pivots, the theoretical mean is about 10,986 comparisons. Individual runs vary. Check many independent runs if estimating the mean, and distinguish comparison counts from elapsed time, which also includes allocation, recursion and machine effects.

## Understand what randomisation changes

On sorted distinct input, always choosing the first element repeatedly creates the most unbalanced partition. Uniform random pivots remove that systematic dependence on input order in expectation. They do not prevent a sequence of extreme pivots by chance.

The teaching implementation can still have quadratic work and deep recursion. Equal keys also all enter one side in this two-way partition, so the distinct-key guarantee does not apply to them. An adaptive adversary or predictable random choices changes the assumptions too.

Production sorts can use duplicate-aware partitioning, depth limits and a fallback algorithm such as heapsort to provide stronger safeguards. Evaluate the actual library contract and implementation rather than assuming it is this teaching function.

## Key takeaways
- A single run checks behaviour, not an expectation or bound.
- Random pivots improve expected behaviour on fixed distinct-key inputs.
- Duplicate handling and fallback strategies address risks outside that expectation.

## Further reading
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/)

lessons.title: Size Bloom filters and respect randomness limits
lessons.summary: An insert-only Bloom filter trades space for false positives.
lessons.body:
A **Bloom filter** can cheaply rule out membership, but a positive answer means “possibly present”. It is useful when a false positive merely triggers a more expensive exact lookup.

## Why the two answers differ

Insertion sets several hash-selected bits. Querying checks the same positions. If any required bit is unset, the key was not inserted. If all are set, other keys may have set them, so membership still needs confirmation.

No false negatives requires an insert-only filter, consistent hash mappings and no lost updates. Clearing a shared bit to delete one key can break that guarantee for other keys. An ordinary Bloom filter therefore cannot support deletion by simply clearing its bits.

## Balance memory and hash work

More bits per inserted key reduces crowding. More hash functions initially help distinguish queries, but too many set too many bits and increase false positives. The usual large-filter ideal-hashing approximation gives a useful sizing rule:

```formula reference
P(B = 0) = (1 − 1/m)^{k × n}
P(B = 0) ≈ e^{−(kn) / m}
FPR ≈ (1 − e^{−(kn) / m})^k
k_opt ≈ (m / n) × ln(2)
where
P: probability of measurable events, dimensionless and between zero and one
m: the positive integer number of bits in an initially empty insert-only filter with independent uniform insertion and absent-query hash positions
n: the positive integer number of distinct keys inserted
k: the positive integer number of hash functions (positions selected per key)
B: the value of one particular bit after all inserts
P(B = 0): the probability that bit is still 0
e: Euler's number, about 2.718
FPR: the false positive rate, the chance an absent key's k bits are all set
k_opt: the optimal positive real hash count under the large-filter approximation; compare neighbouring positive integers for implementation
ln(2): the natural logarithm of 2, about 0.693
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the more bits per key, the fewer bits are set and the rarer false positives become; about 0.7 hash functions per bit-per-key is best.
```

Under that approximation, ten bits per distinct key and seven hash functions give about a 0.82% false-positive rate. The query hash positions are independently sampled in this model, but the events that their selected bits are set are not generally independent after averaging over random insertions. Repeated positions can also test the same bit. The result is therefore not an exact finite-filter probability.

Check actual insertion count and query workload. Inserting beyond the planned count fills more bits and raises false positives. Memory, hash computation and the cost of unnecessary exact lookups all affect the useful design.

Security-sensitive randomness also needs an appropriate source. Python's pseudo-random `random` module is suitable for teaching simulations, not security tokens; use a cryptographic source such as its `secrets` module for those.

## Key takeaways
- Negative answers can rule out membership under stated implementation conditions.
- Positive answers need exact confirmation when correctness matters.
- More hashes help only up to a trade-off point.

## Further reading
- [On the false-positive rate of Bloom filters — Bose and colleagues](https://people.scs.carleton.ca/~michiel/bloomfilter.pdf)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/)

lessons.title: Compare mean and median latency
lessons.summary: A mean reflects totals and outliers; a median describes the centre.
lessons.body:
A latency average should answer a specific question. The **arithmetic mean** reflects totals; the **median** describes the middle observation. Neither alone describes the slow tail.

## One timeout changes the story

Suppose 99 requests take 10 milliseconds and one takes 5,000 milliseconds. The mean is 59.9 milliseconds, while the median is 10 milliseconds. Most requests are still fast, but the timeout contributes strongly to total elapsed latency across the requests.

The mean is the total of the observations divided by their count. The median sorts them and takes the middle value, conventionally averaging the two middle values for an even-sized numeric sample. Weighting each distinct latency equally would ignore how often each occurred.

## Choose the summary for the decision

For total resource work, mean resource use per request is useful: multiplied by request count it gives the total. Wall-clock latency includes waiting and is not automatically CPU service time, so mean latency alone does not determine machine capacity.

The median is robust to a small number of extreme observations. That makes it useful for typical experience, but also means a median dashboard can hide painful timeouts. Conversely, a higher mean does not imply most requests became slower.

Use appropriate tail percentiles or threshold exceedance rates alongside the centre. Record time windows and populations consistently so a change in traffic mix does not masquerade as a change in each request's behaviour.

## Key takeaways
- A few extreme values can move the mean while leaving the median unchanged.
- Means, medians and tail measures answer different questions.
- Distinguish elapsed latency from resource service time.

## Further reading
- [Engineering Statistics Handbook — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/)

lessons.title: Compute percentiles and understand fan-out tails
lessons.summary: State the sample percentile convention and allow ties.
lessons.body:
A **percentile** is a threshold in a distribution, not an average of its tail. Under the empirical **nearest-rank** convention, at least the requested percentage of observations are at or below that threshold. Ties can put more there.

## State the convention

The nearest-rank rule sorts observations, rounds the percentage rank upwards and selects that observation. This implementation extends the rule at zero by returning the minimum:

```python
import math
from fractions import Fraction

def percentile(xs, p):
    # Nearest rank; p=0 returns minimum.
    s = sorted(xs)
    if not s or not 0 <= p <= 100:
        raise ValueError("invalid input")
    # Fraction avoids rank rounding drift.
    k = math.ceil(
        Fraction(str(p)) * len(s) / 100
    )
    return s[max(k - 1, 0)]

lat = [12, 15, 11, 240, 14,
       13, 16, 12, 900, 14]
print(percentile(lat, 50))  # 14
print(percentile(lat, 90))  # 240
```

Some other conventions interpolate between observations. Small samples can therefore produce different answers. A percentile also describes observed spread, not confidence about a population parameter. A p99.9 from only 500 observations is effectively at the sample maximum and provides weak evidence about the population tail.

## Combine distributions, not percentile values

Averaging per-server p99 values does not produce fleet p99. Servers can have different traffic volumes and different distributions that the single percentile hides. Merge raw observations, histograms with compatible buckets or compatible quantile sketches over the same window, then estimate the combined percentile. Histograms and sketches retain representation error.

## Fan-out changes the user experience

If a page waits for every backend, any slow required backend can delay it. With independent calls, the chance all are fast is the product of their fast probabilities; its complement is the chance at least one is slow.

With 100 independent calls each having a 1% slow-event probability, about 63% of pages encounter a slow call. This is an explicit probability assumption: ties mean exceeding an empirical p99 need not occur exactly 1% of the time.

Reducing unnecessary fan-out can help. Hedged requests send a delayed backup and use the first acceptable result, but add load and require suitable request semantics. Correlated backend delays need a different probability model.

## Key takeaways
- Percentiles need a convention, adequate data and attention to ties.
- Combine observations or compatible summaries before computing fleet percentiles.
- Waiting for many backends amplifies opportunities for tail delays.

## Further reading
- [The Tail at Scale — Dean and Barroso](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)
- [Histograms and summaries — Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/)

lessons.title: Estimate uncertainty with standard errors and intervals
lessons.summary: The standard error scales with the inverse square root of the iid sample size.
lessons.body:
The spread of individual requests and the uncertainty in an estimated mean are different. **Standard deviation** describes individual variation; **standard error** describes variation of the estimator across repeated samples.

## More independent data reduces uncertainty

For independent identically distributed observations with finite variance, the standard error of the sample mean decreases with the square root of sample size. Quadrupling observations halves it; doubling observations does not.

```formula essential
SE = σ / √(n)
where
SE: the standard error, the typical distance between the sample mean x̄ and the true mean μ (mu)
σ: sigma, the standard deviation of a single observation, in the same units as the data
n: the positive integer number of independent identically distributed observations
√: the square root
In words: for independent identically distributed observations with finite variance, the sample mean's standard deviation is the individual standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size.
```

This scaling describes sampling variability, not a guaranteed realised error. More observations also cannot remove systematic sampling bias or repair an unrepresentative measurement window.

## Interpret an interval as a procedure

A **95% confidence interval** comes from a procedure intended to cover the fixed true value in 95% of repeated experiments under its assumptions. It is not a statement that 95% of individual requests lie inside, or that this one fixed interval has a 95% posterior probability of containing the parameter.

```formula reference
x̄ ± 1.96 × SE
where
x̄: "x-bar", the sample mean
±: plus or minus; the interval runs from x̄ − 1.96 × SE to x̄ + 1.96 × SE
SE: the standard error of the mean
1.96: the number of standard errors that captures the middle 95% of a normal distribution (2.5% is cut off in each tail)
In words: take the estimate and go about two standard errors either side.
```

The normal approximation requires a sufficiently accurate sampling approximation. A mean estimated from normal iid observations can use a Student-t interval when the standard deviation is estimated. For proportions, the simple Wald interval can perform poorly near zero or one or with few successes or failures; Wilson or exact binomial procedures offer alternatives.

## Check what counts as independent evidence

Many requests during one shared pause may provide less information than the same number spread across independent conditions. Positive correlation can make an independence-based standard error too small; the sign and structure of dependence matter.

Benchmark warm-up, noisy neighbours and changing conditions also matter. Repeat and interleave comparisons rather than giving every observation of one version an earlier environment. A narrow interval under a wrong sampling model can be misleading.

## Key takeaways
- Standard error concerns an estimator, not individual spread.
- Confidence coverage belongs to the repeated procedure.
- Sample size does not fix bias, dependence or a poor approximation.

## Further reading
- [Engineering Statistics Handbook — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/)

lessons.title: Interpret an A/B hypothesis test
lessons.summary: A p-value conditions on the null model rather than assigning it a posterior probability.
lessons.body:
An **A/B test** randomly assigns users to control and variant groups and compares a chosen metric. Randomisation balances other factors in expectation, not perfectly in every realised experiment.

## Ask what the null model predicts

The **null hypothesis** commonly says the variant has no effect. A test statistic measures the observed discrepancy from that model. A **p-value** is the probability, assuming the null and sampling model, of a statistic at least as extreme in the pre-specified direction or directions.

A pre-planned one-sided p-value of 0.03 means such an extreme result would occur about 3% of the time under the null model. It does not mean a 3% probability that the null is true, a 97% probability the variant helps, or a 3% effect size.

## Distinguish decisions from truth

A significance level is a planned bound on false rejection under the test assumptions. A significant result can be a **Type I error**: rejecting a true null. Failing to reject when a real effect exists is a **Type II error**. **Power** is the chance of rejecting under a specified real effect.

Actual error rates depend on the procedure and assumptions. Discrete tests can be conservative; approximations can be inaccurate. Report the effect estimate and uncertainty as well as significance.

## Interpret an inconclusive result

Suppose a planned two-sided test reports a p-value of 0.058 against a 0.05 threshold. It has not met that rule for rejecting the null. That does not establish no effect: the data may be too noisy for the effect size of interest.

Do not keep extending an ordinary fixed-sample test until it crosses the threshold. Use the planned design or an appropriate sequential procedure. Likewise, a statistically significant tiny change may still be too small to justify implementation costs.

## Key takeaways
- P-values condition on a null model; they do not assign it a posterior probability.
- Failure to reject is not proof of no effect.
- Power, effect size and practical value remain separate questions.

## Further reading
- [Engineering Statistics Handbook — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/)

lessons.title: Plan an A/B sample size
lessons.summary: Choose effect size, significance and power before collecting the sample.
lessons.body:
Before collecting an A/B sample, decide how small an effect matters. A study can be large enough to detect a major change yet too noisy to resolve a smaller one.

## Specify the design inputs

Choose the primary metric, expected baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, significance level, desired power and allocation between arms. For a conversion rate, distinguish percentage points from relative change: moving from 10% to 11% is one percentage point and a 10% relative increase.

Power is the chance the planned test detects a specified real effect under the model. An 80% target is a design choice, not a promise that the experiment will show significance or that a significant result is 80% likely to be real.

## Small effects require much more data

At similar variance and fixed significance and power, halving the target effect approximately quadruples the required sample. Sampling noise shrinks with the square root of sample size, so reducing that noise by half takes about four times the data.

The following approximation is a reference for equal-sized independent conversion-rate arms near a shared baseline, two-sided 5% significance and 80% power:

```formula reference
n ≈ (16p(1 − p)) / δ^2
where
n: users per arm
p: the baseline conversion probability, strictly between zero and one
δ: delta, the positive absolute probability difference to detect, not a relative percentage change
16: about 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)^2 = 15.7, rounded up; it bakes in 5% significance and 80% power
≈: approximately equal to
In words: For this approximate equal-arm design, required users per arm grow with outcome variance and with the inverse square of the target absolute difference.
```

Use an appropriate planning method for the actual test, baseline and allocation. This shortcut is not an exact power guarantee, especially with rare outcomes or small samples.

## Plan a feasible experiment

Translate users per arm into duration at available traffic, allowing for the intended sampling unit and relevant cycles. If the needed sample exceeds a stable experiment window, reconsider the detectable effect or design. Reading a visible trend does not create missing information.

Pre-specify the stopping plan. A valid sequential design can use a different stopping rule, but repeatedly extending an ordinary fixed-sample test changes its error properties.

## Key takeaways
- Plan around an effect that matters, stated in clear units.
- Smaller effects usually require much larger samples.
- Sample-size approximations and stopping rules depend on the design.

## Further reading
- [Engineering Statistics Handbook — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/)

lessons.title: Avoid peeking and multiple-testing traps
lessons.summary: Ordinary fixed-sample tests do not retain error control under arbitrary optional stopping.
lessons.body:
A small p-value only has its intended meaning under the analysis and sampling plan. Repeated looks, many metrics and broken assignment can undermine a convincing-looking dashboard.

## Stop according to a valid rule

Repeatedly checking an ordinary fixed-sample p-value and stopping at the first crossing can inflate false positives. Cumulative looks reuse data and are dependent, so neither the nominal threshold nor a formula for independent tests gives a universal overall rate.

Choose a sample size and planned analysis, or use a sequential method with error control appropriate to its stopping and sampling rules. Merely counting the number of looks does not specify the error rate.

## Account for multiple opportunities to win

Testing many metrics increases opportunities for false rejection. The precise risk depends on their dependence and individual test error rates. Declare a primary metric in advance and distinguish confirmatory claims from exploration.

The **Bonferroni correction** allocates a family significance budget among the tests and controls the chance of any false rejection without requiring independence. **False discovery rate** control instead targets the expected fraction of false rejections among rejections; procedures such as Benjamini–Hochberg have their own dependence conditions.

## Check the experiment before interpreting treatment

- **Sample ratio mismatch:** an allocation far from the planned split may reveal assignment, eligibility or logging problems. An appropriate allocation test supplies evidence to investigate, not proof of a specific defect.
- **Novelty and learning effects:** a short-lived response to something new may differ from sustained behaviour. Plan duration around relevant cycles; full weeks do not guarantee these effects have settled.
- **Simpson’s paradox:** uneven segment mixtures can reverse an aggregate comparison. Randomisation balances pre-treatment groups in expectation, while attrition and conditioning on post-treatment outcomes can disturb comparisons.
- **Practical significance:** a detectable effect may still be too small to justify its cost. Report effect size and uncertainty.

## Key takeaways
- Repeated stopping opportunities require a suitable analysis.
- Multiple metrics and allocation checks belong in the design.
- A statistical result still needs a practical interpretation.

## Further reading
- [Engineering Statistics Handbook — NIST](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/)
